# ADR-000: Decision Title

<!--
STARTER KIT GUIDANCE

This file is a TEMPLATE for Architecture and Engineering Decision Records.

When creating an actual ADR:

1. Copy this file.
2. Rename it using the next sequential ADR number and a short descriptive title.

Example:

ADR-001-use-postgresql-for-persistence.md

3. Replace all placeholder text with actual project decision evidence.
4. Delete all instructional HTML comments from the completed ADR.
5. Keep sections that are relevant to understanding the decision.
6. Do not create ADRs for routine implementation details.

A decision record should preserve WHY a meaningful engineering choice was made,
not merely state what the implementation happens to contain.
-->

## Context

<!--
TEAM CONTENT REQUIRED

Explain the engineering problem or decision that requires resolution.

Describe the forces that make the decision meaningful.

Consider relevant:

- requirements;
- acceptance criteria;
- architectural constraints;
- assumptions;
- risks;
- quality attributes;
- operational concerns;
- technical limitations;
- stakeholder needs; and
- existing system conditions.

A reviewer should understand WHY a decision was necessary before reading the
decision itself.

Do not simply restate the selected solution.
-->

## Decision

<!--
TEAM CONTENT REQUIRED

State clearly what the team decided.

The decision should be precise enough that an engineer reviewing the repository
later can understand the selected direction without reconstructing it from
source code.

Where useful, explain:

- the selected approach;
- important boundaries;
- important conditions or limitations; and
- when the decision becomes effective.

Do not put the reasoning for rejecting alternatives only in this section.
Preserve that reasoning under Alternatives Considered.
-->

## Alternatives Considered

<!--
TEAM CONTENT REQUIRED

Document meaningful alternatives the team seriously considered.

Do not invent alternatives after the fact merely to make the ADR appear more
complete.

For each alternative, explain:

- what the alternative was;
- relevant advantages;
- relevant disadvantages or risks; and
- why it was not selected.

Two alternatives are shown below as structural examples only.

Rename, add, or remove subsections as appropriate.
-->

## Consequences

<!--
TEAM CONTENT REQUIRED

Record the important consequences of the decision.

Consequences are not limited to advantages.

Include meaningful:

- benefits;
- costs;
- complexity;
- risks;
- limitations;
- maintenance implications;
- security implications;
- testing implications;
- operational implications; and
- future constraints.

A good ADR makes tradeoffs visible rather than presenting the selected option
as having no downside.
-->

## Evidence

<!--
TEAM CONTENT REQUIRED

Reference repository-visible evidence that informed or supports the decision.

Examples may include:

- requirement IDs;
- acceptance criteria;
- assumptions or open questions;
- risk entries;
- issues;
- pull requests;
- experiments;
- prototypes;
- benchmarks;
- architecture diagrams;
- API contracts;
- tests;
- external technical documentation; or
- other engineering evidence.

Use repository paths, IDs, or links when practical.

Do not claim evidence that does not exist.
-->

## Revisit Conditions

<!--
TEAM CONTENT REQUIRED

State what future evidence or condition would justify reconsidering this
decision.

Examples:

- a requirement changes;
- expected scale increases materially;
- a dependency becomes unsupported;
- performance evidence fails an agreed threshold;
- a security constraint changes;
- operational evidence reveals an unacceptable limitation;
- a previously unvalidated assumption is invalidated.

Avoid vague statements such as:

"Revisit if needed."

If the decision is not expected to require reconsideration under any currently
foreseeable condition, state that explicitly and explain why.
-->

FINAL STARTER KIT CHECK — DELETE FROM COMPLETED ADR

Before committing an actual ADR:

1. Replace ADR-000 and "Decision Title."
2. Replace all metadata placeholders.
3. Complete Context.
4. State the Decision clearly.
5. Document real Alternatives Considered.
6. Record both positive consequences and meaningful tradeoffs.
7. Link supporting Evidence.
8. Define Revisit Conditions.
9. Remove placeholder bullets.
10. Remove all instructional HTML comments.

The completed ADR should read as an engineering decision record, not as a
